subject: Astronomy & Space
title: White Dwarfs: Stellar Embers
description: A fast breakdown of White Dwarfs: Stellar Embers for builders.

hook.text: A white dwarf packs a Sun's worth of mass into a sphere the size of Earth. A teaspoon would weigh 5 tons.

buildup.text: They're the remains of Sun-like stars after shedding their outer layers. No fusion burns—they just slowly cool.

discovery.text: Sirius B was the first white dwarf discovered—a tiny, faint companion to the brightest star in the sky.

twist.text: White dwarfs are made of degenerate matter. Electrons resist further collapse through quantum pressure.

climax.text: They cool over billions of years, eventually fading into dark, cold black dwarfs. None exist yet—the universe is too young.

punchline.text: A Sun compressed to Earth's size. Cooling for eternity.

quiz.question: What prevents a white dwarf from collapsing further?
options: Quantum electron degeneracy pressure resists further compression
Nuclear fusion at the core pushes outward
Magnetic fields inside the star hold it up

details.summary: White dwarfs are the dense, Earth-sized remnants of Sun-like stars after they shed their outer layers. With no fusion occurring, they slowly cool over billions of years like cosmic embers.
details.whyItMatters: White dwarfs are the final state of 97% of all stars, including our Sun. They serve as cosmic clocks — their cooling rate helps astronomers measure the age of star clusters and the galaxy itself.
takeaways: White dwarfs are Earth-sized remnants of Sun-like stars
They cool slowly over billions of years without fusion
Electron degeneracy pressure prevents further collapse

faq.question: How dense are white dwarfs?
faq.answer: A teaspoon of white dwarf material weighs about 5.5 tons. They pack roughly the Sun's mass into Earth's volume. This extreme density is supported by electron degeneracy pressure — the quantum mechanical resistance of electrons to being compressed further.

faq.question: What is the Chandrasekhar limit?
faq.answer: The maximum mass for a white dwarf is about 1.4 solar masses, calculated by Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Above this limit, electron degeneracy pressure cannot support the star against gravity. White dwarfs exceeding this limit (through accretion) collapse or explode as Type Ia supernovae.
